procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge convicted all four accused. The High Court maintained the conviction of only the two appellants.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the trial was illegal and void because they were prosecuted for non-cognizable offences. The Supreme Court rejected this argument and found no error in the High Court's or Sessions Judge's appreciation of the evidence, dismissing the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails, and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial for offences under s. 120B, read with ss. 467/471 and 420 IPC, is illegal and void for want of sanction under s. 196-A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because the object of the conspiracy included the commission of non-cognizable offences (ss. 467/471 IPC).

facts: The appellants were charged with criminal conspiracy (s. 120B IPC) to commit both a cognizable offence (cheating under s. 420 IPC) and non-cognizable offences (forgery under ss. 467/471 IPC).
The prosecution did not obtain the prior sanction required under s. 196-A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecuting a conspiracy to commit non-cognizable offences.
The appellants argued that this lack of sanction made the entire trial illegal and void.
law: Under s. 196-A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court cannot take cognizance of a criminal conspiracy to commit a non-cognizable offence without prior sanction from the specified authorities.
No such sanction is required for a conspiracy to commit a cognizable offence, such as cheating under s. 420 IPC.
application: The Court held that the key to resolving the issue is to determine the main "object of the conspiracy."
It found that the object must be determined by reading the charges as a whole, not just by looking at the sections of the law cited.
In this case, the Court concluded that the sole object of the conspiracy was to cheat banks and post offices to obtain money (the cognizable offence under s. 420 IPC).
The commission of the non-cognizable offences of forgery (ss. 467/471) was not the end goal, but merely the "means adopted" or "steps taken" by the accused to achieve the main object of cheating.

The Court reasoned that the accused would not have been satisfied by simply forging documents; their ultimate purpose was to use those documents to dishonestly induce the authorities to part with money.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument and held that the trial was not illegal. It decided that when the main object of a criminal conspiracy is to commit a cognizable offence (cheating), no sanction is required under s. 196-A(2), even if non-cognizable offences (forgery) are committed as a means to achieve that main object.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court and the Sessions Judge erred in the appreciation of evidence to find the appellants guilty of the offences.

facts: The appellants raised two contentions before the High Court and the Supreme Court.
The second contention was that the evidence presented by the prosecution was insufficient to establish their guilt, and therefore the lower courts erred in their appreciation of the evidence.
law: The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with the appreciation of evidence by lower courts, especially when there are concurrent findings of fact by both the trial court (Sessions Judge) and the appellate court (High Court), unless a clear error is demonstrated.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the issue of evidence appreciation relates to the merits of the case.
It observed that both the Sessions Judge and the High Court had already "very elaborately gone into the evidence" concerning the appellants.
Based on that detailed examination of the evidence, both lower courts had found the appellants guilty of the offences.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no error in the way the High Court or the Sessions Judge had appreciated the evidence. Therefore, it concluded there was no justification for it to interfere with their findings and rejected this contention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial for offences under s. 120B, read with ss. 467/471 and 420 IPC, is illegal and void for want of sanction under s. 196-A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because the object of the conspiracy included the commission of non-cognizable offences (ss. 467/471 IPC).
appellant_arguments: The trial was illegal and void because the accused were prosecuted for non-cognizable offences (ss. 467/471 IPC) as part of the conspiracy charge, and the necessary sanction under s. 196A of the Code had not been obtained.
The fact that the accused were also tried for a cognizable offence (cheating under s. 420 IPC) does not make the trial valid.
A joint trial for cognizable and non-cognizable offences, under these circumstances, is illegal and void.
respondent_arguments: The main object of the conspiracy was to cheat banks and post offices, which is a cognizable offence under s. 420 IPC.
The forgeries committed on cheques and postal orders (non-cognizable offences under ss. 467/471 IPC) were only incidental to the main object of cheating.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court and the Sessions Judge erred in the appreciation of evidence to find the appellants guilty of the offences.
appellant_arguments: The High Court and the Sessions Judge erred in their appreciation of the evidence in the case.
respondent_arguments: The conviction was based on a proper and elaborate appreciation of evidence by both the Sessions Judge and the High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When the object of a criminal conspiracy is to commit non-cognizable offenses, sanction under Section 196A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessary, and a trial for such an offense without sanction is neither illegal nor void.
obiter: The decision in Madan Lal v. State of Punjab does not assist the appellant's case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The object of a conspiracy must be determined by reading the charges themselves, not just by looking at the penal sections cited. In this case, the charges show the sole object of the conspiracy was to cheat banks and post offices, a cognizable offence. The non-cognizable offences of forgery and using forged documents were not the ultimate goal but were merely the means adopted by the accused to realize the object of cheating. Therefore, a trial for a conspiracy whose main object is a cognizable offence does not require sanction under s. 196-A(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, even if non-cognizable offences are committed as part of the scheme.
legal_tests_applied: The object of the conspiracy has to be determined. not only by reference to the sections of th~ penal cnac.ment, referred to in the charge but on a reading of the charges themselves.
why_appellant_lost: The court determined that the non-cognizable offences of forgery (ss. 467/471 IPC) were not the object of the conspiracy; rather, they were only the means to achieve the ultimate object, which was cheating (s. 420 IPC).

The accused would not be satisfied by merely en'.ering into a conspiracy to forge the postal orders or the cheques, or even to use such forged documents. The forging of the documents and using such forged documents, were only means adopted by the accused for realising the object, of the conspiracy, which was to cheat.

On the issue of evidence, the Supreme Court deferred to the concurrent findings of the lower courts, stating: 'We do not see any error, committed by the High Court, or the Sessions Judge, in the appreciation of the evidence, in the case, and there is no .justification for any interfer-ence, by this Court.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the argument that the only object of the conspiracy was to cheat the banks and post offices, which is a cognizable offence under s. 420 IPC for which no sanction is necessary.

The principle that sanction under s. 196A is not necessary when the main object of a conspiracy is to commit a cognizable offence, even if non-cognizable offences are used as a means, is supported by a line of previous judicial decisions.
The conviction was upheld because both the Sessions Judge and the High Court had 'very elaborately gone into the evidence regarding the appellants, and have found them guilty of the offences'.
